result.title: Evidence for contact delocalization in atomic scale friction

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study analyzes a two-spring model to explain fine structure in Friction Force Microscopy (FFM) data. It proposes that the tip apex can be delocalized due to rapid thermally activated motion. This model challenges the traditional Tomlinson model, which is based on a single spring, for atomic friction.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study presents a theoretical analysis of a two-mass-two-spring system to explain fine structure in slip events observed in Friction Force Microscopy (FFM). It proposes that the tip apex mass is ultra-low, leading to contact delocalization that affects the measured friction dynamics. A hybrid computational method combining Langevin and Monte-Carlo simulations was used to model the interplay between the fast tip motion and slow cantilever response.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The text defines the mathematical model for a one-dimensional two-mass system, specifying the potential energy and equations of motion for the cantilever and tip apex. It introduces the Tomlinson parameter to determine the number of potential wells and the conditions for thermally activated jumps. A hybrid numerical method combining a Langevin equation for the cantilever and a Monte-Carlo algorithm for tip transitions is described, including the treatment of damping and noise.

knowledge_units.context_summary: In the two-well regime, the tip apex delocalizes due to rapid thermal jumps, causing the cantilever to move in an effective potential defined by the mean tip position. The mean surface force is reduced and the effective potential is flattened due to the competition between increasing potential energy and entropy from apex disorder. Discontinuities in the mean force correspond to transitions between one-well and two-well potential shapes, occurring over a timescale determined by the jump rates.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The text validates the two-mass model against experimental data, noting that single slip events occur at both high and very low surface corrugations. It identifies a discrepancy in slip duration, attributing it to non-sinusoidal surface potentials with wider barriers. The analysis constrains the effective contact mass to less than 10^-18 kg based on the presence of intermediate slip states.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The text discusses how contact delocalization can occur at any cantilever position in specific regimes, necessitating a re-evaluation of standard Friction Force Microscopy (FFM) interpretations. It identifies the rapid movement of the tip in the GHz range as the key factor for energy transfer, which is made possible by the generation of phonons within the tip or between the tip and the substrate. The results suggest that local surface deformation can cause significant thermally induced movements during macroscopic friction.
